The estimated distribution of $J_{b}$ ends up concentrated in a band that is quite reasonable for SAG operation, with a median close to the center of the cloud and a relatively tight interquartile range. This is a good sign, since, despite the temporal noise observed in the series, the model is not pushing most of the estimates toward extreme values nor piling them up artificially at the physical limits. The unimodal shape suggests that, over the period analyzed, the mill operated most of the time around a dominant ball-charge regime, with deviations toward lower or higher values that may be associated with campaign changes, media wear, ball additions, ore variability, or operational transients. From the metallurgical standpoint, this histogram is useful as a plausibility check. If the center of mass of the distribution were too low, we would suspect an underestimation of ball inventory or a loss of sensitivity in the pressure proxy; if it were too high, we might be confusing ore/slurry charge with media charge. In this case, the distribution suggests a reasonably stable calibrated model, although its practical use should always be complemented with actual records of ball consumption and addition.


### Computing the filling ratio

All that remains is to compute the SAG mill's filling ratio: $\Gamma_{b} =J_{b}/J_{c}$. As we commented earlier, this ratio is an indicator of the mill's filling efficiency and is useful in operational control, since it lets us identify whether the mill is operating with an appropriate proportion of balls relative to the total charge volume:

```{python}
# We compute the filling ratio.
df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"] = df_filt["calc_jb_cal_sag"] / df_filt["calc_jc_cal_sag"]
df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"] = (
    df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"]
    .apply(lambda x: x if np.isfinite(x) and (x >= 0.0) else np.nan)
)

# We check that jb/jc <= 1. If not, we set jb/jc = 1 to simulate a mill
# completely full of balls ("grind-out" case).
df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"] = np.where(
    df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"] > 1.0,
    1.0,
    df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"],
)
```

Next, we visually inspect the evolution of the estimated filling ratio, $\Gamma_{b}$, across the different campaigns:

```{python}
#| label: fig-sag-filling-ratio-time-series
#| fig-cap: "Evolution of the Jb/Jc filling ratio. The series reveals changes in the relative composition of grinding media and total charge between campaigns."
# We initialize the figure.
fig = go.Figure()

# We add the evolution of the estimated ball fill level (jb) over campaign time.
# We resample every 4h for greater visual clarity.
fig.add_trace(
    go.Scatter(
        x=df_filt.resample("4h", on="timestamp").mean().index,
        y=df_filt.resample("4h", on="timestamp").mean()["calc_jb_jc_sag"],
        mode="lines",
        name="Filling ratio (jb/jc)",
        line=dict(color="firebrick", width=2, shape="hv"),
    ),
)

# We configure the figure layout.
fig.update_layout(
    title="<b>Jb/Jc filling ratio</b>",
    title_font=dict(size=20, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
    title_subtitle=dict(
        text="Estimation based on the H&F model and the internal charge balance",
        font=dict(size=14, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
    ),
    height=500,
    margin=dict(t=110),
)

fig.update_yaxes(
    title_text="<b>Filling ratio (jb/jc)</b>",
    title_font=dict(size=16, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
    dtick=0.1,
)

show_plotly(fig)
```

The time series of $\Gamma_{b} = J_{b}/J_{c}$ shows that the relative composition of the internal charge does not stay fixed during the campaigns, but oscillates within a wide band, with episodes where balls account for close to half of the total fill and others where they come to dominate a large part of the effective charge. From an operational standpoint, this is expected if we remember that $J_{c}$ responds to the mill's total charge, while $J_{b}$ is conditioned by media wear, discrete ball replenishment, ore changes, feed transients, and the quality of the pressure proxy. Very high values, close to 1, should be read with care: Physically they would indicate a charge almost entirely dominated by steel media, something that may appear as a clipping effect, an underestimation of ore/slurry charge, or transient conditions rather than as a desirable permanent state. In metallurgical terms, the usefulness of the chart lies in detecting regime changes: When $\Gamma_{b}$ rises steadily, the mill could be operating with greater impact intensity but also with higher specific consumption and wear; when it drops too far, it may lose breakage capacity from media and depend more on autogenous mechanisms, with a risk of coarse material building up. Therefore, this ratio should not be used as an isolated setpoint, but as an indicator of internal composition to be contrasted against throughput, power, pressure, grinding noise, product particle size, and actual ball-addition records.

Now, the filling ratio becomes much more useful when we stop looking at it as an isolated time series and start crossing it with outcome variables. In particular, we want to know which regions of the plane defined by $\Gamma_b$ and mill power concentrate higher throughput levels. The metallurgical intuition is straightforward: for the same power, different internal charge compositions can produce very different grinding rates. A charge with a low relative proportion of balls may consume energy without generating enough effective impact; a charge with an excessive proportion of balls may increase impacts and wear, but reduce the useful space for ore and slurry. For this reason, we will look for throughput isocontours in the filling-ratio--power plane, in order to identify candidate operating bands for different campaigns.

The following function replicates the logic used earlier to study power and pressure, but now dispenses with the scatter plot. In its place, it builds a bivariate grid where each cell contains the average throughput observed for a combination of filling ratio and power. On that surface we draw a color gradient and isocontour lines, which lets us visually locate regions of equivalent throughput:

```{python}
def plot_filling_ratio_domain(campaign_index: int):
    """
    Function that plots throughput isocontours in the plane
    formed by the pair (filling ratio, power) for a specific
    campaign.
    """
    # We select the campaign indicated by index.
    CAMPAIGN_INIT = reliner_data["init_date"].iloc[campaign_index]
    CAMPAIGN_END = reliner_data["end_date"].iloc[campaign_index]

    # We filter the campaign and clean up spurious operating conditions.
    campaign_data = df_filt[
        (df_filt["timestamp"] >= CAMPAIGN_INIT)
        & (df_filt["timestamp"] <= CAMPAIGN_END)
        & (df_filt["sag_power_kw"] > POWER_THRESHOLD)
        & (df_filt["fresh_feed_tph"] > THROUGHPUT_THRESH)
        & (df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"] > 0.0)
        & (df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"] <= 1.0)
    ].copy()

    # We resample to 4 hours to stay consistent with the earlier
    # charts and reduce very high-frequency noise.
    plot_data = (
        campaign_data
        .resample("4h", on="timestamp")
        .mean()
        .reset_index()
        [["calc_jb_jc_sag", "sag_power_kw", "fresh_feed_tph"]]
        .dropna()
    )

    # We build a discrete grid: filling ratio vs power.
    N_BINS = 28
    plot_data = plot_data.assign(
        ratio_bin=pd.cut(plot_data["calc_jb_jc_sag"], bins=N_BINS),
        power_bin=pd.cut(plot_data["sag_power_kw"], bins=N_BINS),
    )

    contour_grid = plot_data.pivot_table(
        index="power_bin",
        columns="ratio_bin",
        values="fresh_feed_tph",
        aggfunc="mean",
        observed=False,
    )

    ratio_centers = [interval.mid for interval in contour_grid.columns]
    power_centers = [interval.mid for interval in contour_grid.index]

    # We initialize the figure.
    fig = go.Figure()

    # Map of average throughput and isocontours.
    fig.add_trace(
        go.Contour(
            x=ratio_centers,
            y=power_centers,
            z=contour_grid.to_numpy(),
            colorscale="RdYlGn",
            contours=dict(
                coloring="heatmap",
                showlabels=True,
                labelfont=dict(
                    size=11,
                    color="black",
                    family=PLOTLY_FONT,
                ),
            ),
            line=dict(
                color="black",
                width=1.2,
                dash="dash",
            ),
            connectgaps=True,
            colorbar=dict(
                title=dict(
                    text="<b>Throughput (tph)</b>",
                    side="right",
                    font=dict(size=15, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
                ),
                tickfont=dict(size=12, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
                x=1.02,
                thickness=24,
            ),
            hovertemplate=(
                "<b>Filling ratio</b>: %{x:.2f}<br>"
                "<b>Power</b>: %{y:.0f} kW<br>"
                "<b>Average throughput</b>: %{z:.0f} tph<extra></extra>"
            ),
        )
    )

    # We configure the layout.
    fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(
            text="<b>Throughput isocontours by filling ratio and power</b>",
            font=dict(size=20, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
            x=0.5,
            xanchor="center",
        ),
        title_subtitle=dict(
            text=f"Campaign index {campaign_index} - 4-hour resampling",
            font=dict(size=14, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
        ),
        height=600,
        margin=dict(t=120, r=140),
    )

    fig.update_xaxes(
        title=dict(
            text="<b>Filling ratio (Jb/Jc)</b>",
            font=dict(size=15, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
        ),
    )

    fig.update_yaxes(
        title=dict(
            text="<b>power_kw</b>",
            font=dict(size=15, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
        ),
    )

    return fig
```

Let us look first at the resulting domain for campaign number `1`:

```{python}
#| label: fig-sag-filling-ratio-domain-campaign-1
#| fig-cap: "Control surface of campaign 1. The isocontours locate the combinations of filling ratio and power associated with higher mill throughput."
show_plotly(plot_filling_ratio_domain(campaign_index=1))
```

This chart should be read as an operating surface (or, in more technical jargon, as a **control surface**): Each color represents the average throughput observed for a combination of power and filling ratio, while the black curves connect regions of similar throughput. If the highest-throughput zones concentrate in a narrow band of $\Gamma_{b}$, then the campaign suggests a relatively well-defined charge composition for operating efficiently. If, on the contrary, the maxima appear scattered across several islands, then throughput is probably also being governed by variables we are not plotting directly, such as ore hardness, particle size, water, recirculation, or classification.

Let us repeat the exercise for campaign number `4`, which previously showed more dispersed behavior in the power-pressure map:

```{python}
#| label: fig-sag-filling-ratio-domain-campaign-4
#| fig-cap: "Control surface of campaign 4. The position of its maxima shows that the efficient filling-ratio band depends on the state of the campaign and not on a single universal value."
show_plotly(plot_filling_ratio_domain(campaign_index=4))
```

Comparing campaigns lets us separate structural conditions from transient ones. The same filling ratio can be favorable in one liner campaign and less attractive in another if liner wear, feed characteristics, or control strategy change. For that reason, the practical recommendation is not to choose a single $J_{b}/J_{c}$ ratio for the entire operating history, but to build target bands by liner campaign or family of operating conditions. In control terms, these surfaces help answer a concrete question: For a given power draw, which relative charge composition appears to convert energy into processed tonnes most effectively?

The control surfaces show that the relationship between filling ratio, power, and throughput is neither linear nor unique across campaigns, which is very consistent with a real SAG operation. In campaign index `1`, the throughput maxima appear in several zones: An interesting region around $\Gamma_b \approx 0.85-0.90$ with power close to 11.8-12.2 MW, and another band of good performance toward $\Gamma_b \approx 0.65-0.75$ with higher power, on the order of 13-14 MW. This suggests that the campaign admits more than one efficient regime: One with a higher filling ratio and moderate power, possibly associated with good relative availability of grinding media, and another with higher power where the mill seems to compensate with energy for a different charge composition. In campaign index `4`, by contrast, the surface looks more structured toward a good-throughput zone around $\Gamma_b \approx 0.85-0.92$ and power close to 10.8-12.0 MW, while at higher power throughput does not necessarily improve. From an operational perspective, this is highly relevant: Pushing power does not guarantee maximizing tonnes if the internal charge composition is not in a favorable band. The practical reading would be to use these surfaces to build target bands by campaign, not a universal $J_b/J_c$ recommendation. If one campaign shows high throughput with elevated filling ratios and moderate power, the strategy could aim at sustaining a sufficiently active media charge without energetically overloading the mill; if another campaign requires higher power to reach similar throughput, then hardness, particle size, liner wear, recirculation, or classification conditions are probably coming into play. In short, these surfaces make it possible to transform the filling ratio from a simple calculated indicator into a control tool: They help locate regions where energy converts better into throughput, and distinguish when increasing power is genuinely useful and when it only makes the operation more expensive.

### Exploratory operational-control dashboard

So that the comparison between campaigns is not reduced to two static charts, we can build a small interactive dashboard. The idea is simple: Keep the same control surface, but let the reader switch campaigns with a slider. For each campaign we also show the point of highest average throughput observed in the grid. That point should not be interpreted as an automatic operating recipe, since it may be supported by only a few observations or reflect feed variability or campaign-specific conditions; however, it serves as a quick marker for locating candidate regions of efficient operation.

This dashboard is deliberately sober. It does not try to replace an expert system or a plant optimizer; it only makes it possible to explore a concrete metallurgical question: **For a given liner campaign, which historical combination of filling ratio and power draw converted energy into processed tonnes most effectively?**

```{python}
def build_filling_ratio_surface(
    campaign_index: int,
    n_bins: int = 28,
    min_obs: int = 40,
):
    """
    Builds the average throughput surface for a specific campaign.
    Returns the bin centers and the throughput matrix.
    """
    # We select the start and end of the campaign.
    campaign_init = reliner_data["init_date"].iloc[campaign_index]
    campaign_end = reliner_data["end_date"].iloc[campaign_index]

    # We filter reasonable operating data.
    campaign_data = df_filt[
        (df_filt["timestamp"] >= campaign_init)
        & (df_filt["timestamp"] <= campaign_end)
        & (df_filt["sag_power_kw"] > POWER_THRESHOLD)
        & (df_filt["fresh_feed_tph"] > THROUGHPUT_THRESH)
        & (df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"] > 0.0)
        & (df_filt["calc_jb_jc_sag"] <= 1.0)
    ].copy()

    # We resample to stabilize the operational reading.
    plot_data = (
        campaign_data
        .resample("4h", on="timestamp")
        .mean()
        .reset_index()
        [["calc_jb_jc_sag", "sag_power_kw", "fresh_feed_tph"]]
        .dropna()
    )

    # If the campaign has little data, we do not build a surface.
    if len(plot_data) < min_obs:
        return None

    # We build the discrete grid.
    plot_data = plot_data.assign(
        ratio_bin=pd.cut(plot_data["calc_jb_jc_sag"], bins=n_bins),
        power_bin=pd.cut(plot_data["sag_power_kw"], bins=n_bins),
    )

    contour_grid = plot_data.pivot_table(
        index="power_bin",
        columns="ratio_bin",
        values="fresh_feed_tph",
        aggfunc="mean",
        observed=False,
    )

    # If the grid ends up empty, we discard the campaign.
    if contour_grid.dropna(how="all").empty:
        return None

    ratio_centers = np.array([interval.mid for interval in contour_grid.columns])
    power_centers = np.array([interval.mid for interval in contour_grid.index])
    throughput_grid = contour_grid.to_numpy()

    return ratio_centers, power_centers, throughput_grid

def plot_filling_ratio_dashboard():
    """
    Builds an interactive dashboard for navigating control surfaces
    by campaign.
    """
    # We look for campaigns with enough data to build the surface.
    surfaces = []
    for campaign_index in range(len(reliner_data)):
        surface = build_filling_ratio_surface(campaign_index)
        if surface is not None:
            surfaces.append((campaign_index, *surface))

    # We initialize traces and slider steps.
    traces = []
    steps = []

    for idx, (campaign_index, ratio_x, power_y, grid_z) in enumerate(surfaces):
        visible = idx == 0

        # We locate the point of highest average throughput observed in the grid.
        max_pos = np.unravel_index(np.nanargmax(grid_z), grid_z.shape)
        best_power = power_y[max_pos[0]]
        best_ratio = ratio_x[max_pos[1]]
        best_throughput = grid_z[max_pos]

        # Throughput surface.
        traces.append(
            go.Contour(
                x=ratio_x,
                y=power_y,
                z=grid_z,
                visible=visible,
                colorscale="RdYlGn",
                contours=dict(
                    coloring="heatmap",
                    showlabels=True,
                    labelfont=dict(
                        size=10,
                        color="black",
                        family=PLOTLY_FONT,
                    ),
                ),
                line=dict(color="black", width=1.0, dash="dash"),
                connectgaps=True,
                colorbar=dict(
                    title=dict(
                        text="<b>Throughput (tph)</b>",
                        side="right",
                        font=dict(size=15, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
                    ),
                    tickfont=dict(size=12, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
                    x=1.02,
                    thickness=24,
                ),
                hovertemplate=(
                    "<b>Filling ratio</b>: %{x:.2f}<br>"
                    "<b>Power</b>: %{y:.0f} kW<br>"
                    "<b>Average throughput</b>: %{z:.0f} tph<extra></extra>"
                ),
                name="Throughput surface",
                showscale=True,
            )
        )

        # Point of highest average throughput.
        traces.append(
            go.Scatter(
                x=[best_ratio],
                y=[best_power],
                visible=visible,
                mode="markers+text",
                marker=dict(
                    color="black",
                    size=13,
                    symbol="x",
                    line=dict(color="white", width=2),
                ),
                text=[f"{best_throughput:.0f} tph"],
                textposition="top center",
                textfont=dict(size=12, family=PLOTLY_FONT, color="black"),
                hovertemplate=(
                    "<b>Best historical cell</b><br>"
                    f"<b>Campaign</b>: {campaign_index}<br>"
                    "<b>Filling ratio</b>: %{x:.2f}<br>"
                    "<b>Power</b>: %{y:.0f} kW<br>"
                    f"<b>Average throughput</b>: {best_throughput:.0f} tph"
                    "<extra></extra>"
                ),
                name="Best historical cell",
            )
        )

        # Each step must activate the two traces associated with a campaign.
        visible_mask = [False] * (2 * len(surfaces))
        visible_mask[2 * idx] = True
        visible_mask[2 * idx + 1] = True

        steps.append(
            dict(
                method="update",
                label=f"C{campaign_index}",
                args=[
                    {
                        "visible": visible_mask,
                    },
                    {
                        "title.subtitle.text": (
                            f"Campaign index {campaign_index} - "
                            "4-hour resampling"
                        )
                    },
                ],
            )
        )

    # We assemble the figure.
    fig = go.Figure(data=traces)

    fig.update_layout(
        title=dict(
            text=(
                "<b>Control dashboard: throughput by "
                "filling ratio and power</b>"
            ),
            font=dict(size=20, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
            x=0.5,
            xanchor="center",
        ),
        title_subtitle=dict(
            text=(
                f"Campaign index {surfaces[0][0]} - "
                "4-hour resampling"
            ),
            font=dict(size=14, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
        ),
        sliders=[
            dict(
                active=0,
                currentvalue=dict(
                    prefix="Campaign ",
                    font=dict(size=14, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
                ),
                pad=dict(t=45),
                steps=steps,
            )
        ],
        legend=dict(
            orientation="h",
            x=0.5,
            y=1.06,
            xanchor="center",
            yanchor="bottom",
        ),
        height=680,
        margin=dict(t=130, r=140, b=90),
    )

    fig.update_xaxes(
        title=dict(
            text="<b>Filling ratio (Jb/Jc)</b>",
            font=dict(size=15, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
        ),
    )

    fig.update_yaxes(
        title=dict(
            text="<b>Power (kW)</b>",
            font=dict(size=15, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
        ),
    )

    return fig
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-sag-filling-ratio-dashboard
#| fig-cap: "Interactive dashboard for exploring throughput surfaces by campaign. The controls make it possible to compare robust bands of filling ratio and power, as well as the observational support of each region."
show_plotly(plot_filling_ratio_dashboard())
```

The right way to read this dashboard is campaign by campaign. The black marker indicates the cell with the highest average throughput within the grid, but its value should be understood as a historical reference, not as a direct *set-point*. A very high cell may come from a genuinely favorable condition, but it may also come from a zone with few observations, from softer ore, or from a particularly good transient configuration. That is why, rather than chasing an exact point, it is better to look for **consistent regions**: Bands of filling ratio and power where throughput stays high across several neighboring cells. That spatial stability is far more valuable for operational control than an isolated maximum.

### Comparing the results against the various measurements of $J_{b}$ and $J_{c}$

To close the exercise, let us compare the values estimated by the model against the point measurements available in `actual_vals_data`. This step must be done carefully, since the manual measurements of $J_b$ and $J_c$ do not constitute a continuous series, but rather field observations taken on specific dates. In addition, the file provided with these measurements contains dates without an explicit time, whereas the historian holds high-frequency records. For this reason, we will not compare against the nearest 15-minute point, since that would give a false sense of precision. Instead, we will summarize the model at a daily scale using the median, and we will compare each point measurement against the estimated daily state of the mill for that same date.

```{python}
# We prepare the point field measurements.
actual_compare = actual_vals_data.copy()
actual_compare["timestamp"] = pd.to_datetime(actual_compare["timestamp"]).dt.normalize()

# The actual measurements come expressed as percentages.
actual_compare["actual_jc"] = actual_compare["jc_measured_pct"] / 100.0
actual_compare["actual_jb"] = actual_compare["jb_measured_pct"] / 100.0
actual_compare["actual_jb_jc"] = actual_compare["actual_jb"] / actual_compare["actual_jc"]

# We summarize the model at a daily scale, using robust medians.
model_daily = (
    df_filt
    .resample("D", on="timestamp")
    .median(numeric_only=True)
    .reset_index()
)
model_daily["timestamp"] = model_daily["timestamp"].dt.normalize()

# We keep the columns relevant to the comparison.
model_daily = model_daily[
    [
        "timestamp",
        "calc_jc_cal_sag",
        "calc_jb_cal_sag",
        "calc_jb_jc_sag",
        "sag_power_kw",
        "bearing_pressure_psi",
        "fresh_feed_tph",
    ]
].rename(
    columns={
        "calc_jc_cal_sag": "model_jc",
        "calc_jb_cal_sag": "model_jb",
        "calc_jb_jc_sag": "model_jb_jc",
        "sag_power_kw": "power_kw",
        "bearing_pressure_psi": "pressure_psi",
        "fresh_feed_tph": "throughput_tph",
    }
)

# We join the point measurements with the estimated daily median.
model_vs_actual = (
    actual_compare
    .merge(model_daily, on="timestamp", how="left")
    .dropna(subset=["model_jc", "model_jb"])
)

# We compute estimation errors.
for var_j in ["jc", "jb", "jb_jc"]:
    model_vs_actual[f"error_{var_j}"] = (
        model_vs_actual[f"model_{var_j}"] - model_vs_actual[f"actual_{var_j}"]
    )
    model_vs_actual[f"abs_error_{var_j}"] = model_vs_actual[f"error_{var_j}"].abs()
```

With this we obtain a compact table that lets us inspect each field measurement and its modeled counterpart:

```{python}
cols_to_show = [
    "timestamp",
    "actual_jc",
    "model_jc",
    "error_jc",
    "actual_jb",
    "model_jb",
    "error_jb",
    "actual_jb_jc",
    "model_jb_jc",
    "error_jb_jc",
]

model_vs_actual[cols_to_show].round(4)
```

We also summarize performance through bias, mean absolute error, RMSE, and correlation. Bias is defined as `model - measurement`, so that positive values indicate an average level of overestimation by the model, while negative values indicate underestimation. The mean absolute error (MAE) and the RMSE let us evaluate the magnitude of the errors regardless of their sign, while the correlation indicates how well the model follows the general trend of the point measurements:

```{python}
def summarize_point_comparison(data, var):
    """
    Summarizes the contrast between modeled values and point measurements.
    """
    err = data[f"error_{var}"].dropna()
    actual = data[f"actual_{var}"]
    model = data[f"model_{var}"]

    return {
        "variable": var,
        "n": int(err.shape[0]),
        "bias": np.nanmean(err),
        "mae": np.nanmean(np.abs(err)),
        "rmse": np.sqrt(np.nanmean(err**2)),
        "correlation": actual.corr(model),
    }
```

```{python}
# We build a performance summary for each variable of interest.
comparison_summary = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        summarize_point_comparison(model_vs_actual, "jc"),
        summarize_point_comparison(model_vs_actual, "jb"),
        summarize_point_comparison(model_vs_actual, "jb_jc"),
    ]
)

# And we display it on screen.
comparison_summary.round(4)
```

A direct visualization helps us understand whether the model is following the general trend of the point measurements. In the chart below, each point corresponds to a manual measurement. The dashed line represents the ideal case, where the modeled value coincides exactly with the measured value:

```{python}
#| label: fig-sag-fill-level-point-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Agreement between the Jc, Jb, and Jb/Jc estimates and the point field measurements. The diagonal represents perfect agreement and makes it possible to identify bias and dispersion in each quantity."
# We initialize a comparison figure.
fig = psub.make_subplots(
    rows=1,
    cols=3,
    subplot_titles=(
        "<b>Jc</b>",
        "<b>Jb</b>",
        "<b>Jb/Jc</b>",
    ),
    horizontal_spacing=0.12,
)

fig.update_annotations(font=dict(family=PLOTLY_FONT, size=18))

comparison_specs = [
    {
        "var": "jc",
        "title": "<b>Total fill level</b>",
        "color": "dodgerblue",
        "row": 1,
        "col": 1,
    },
    {
        "var": "jb",
        "title": "<b>Ball level</b>",
        "color": "darkorange",

        "col": 2,
    },
    {
        "var": "jb_jc",
        "title": "<b>Filling ratio</b>",
        "color": "firebrick",
        "row": 1,
        "col": 3,
    },
]

for spec_k in comparison_specs:
    var_k = spec_k["var"]
    row_k = spec_k["row"]
    col_k = spec_k["col"]

    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=model_vs_actual[f"actual_{var_k}"],
            y=model_vs_actual[f"model_{var_k}"],
            mode="markers",
            marker=dict(
                color=spec_k["color"],
                size=9,
                opacity=0.8,
                line=dict(color="black", width=0.8),
            ),
            text=model_vs_actual["timestamp"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"),
            hovertemplate=(
                "<b>Date</b>: %{text}<br>"
                "<b>Measurement</b>: %{x:.3f}<br>"
                "<b>Model</b>: %{y:.3f}<extra></extra>"
            ),
            showlegend=False,
        ),
        row=row_k,
        col=col_k,
    )

    min_axis = np.nanmin(
        [
            model_vs_actual[f"actual_{var_k}"].min(),
            model_vs_actual[f"model_{var_k}"].min(),
        ]
    )
    max_axis = np.nanmax(
        [
            model_vs_actual[f"actual_{var_k}"].max(),
            model_vs_actual[f"model_{var_k}"].max(),
        ]
    )
    axis_pad = 0.05 * (max_axis - min_axis)
    min_axis -= axis_pad
    max_axis += axis_pad

    fig.add_trace(
        go.Scatter(
            x=[min_axis, max_axis],
            y=[min_axis, max_axis],
            mode="lines",
            line=dict(color="black", width=1.2, dash="dash"),
            showlegend=False,
            hoverinfo="skip",
        ),
        row=row_k,
        col=col_k,
    )

    fig.update_xaxes(
        title=dict(
            text="<b>Point measurement</b>",
            font=dict(size=14, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
        ),
        range=[min_axis, max_axis],
        row=row_k,
        col=col_k,
    )

    fig.update_yaxes(
        title=dict(
            text="<b>Model</b>",
            font=dict(size=14, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
        ),
        range=[min_axis, max_axis],
        row=row_k,
        col=col_k,
    )

fig.update_layout(
    title=dict(
        text="<b>Contrast between the model and the point field measurements</b>",
        font=dict(size=20, family=PLOTLY_FONT),
        x=0.5,
        xanchor="center",
    ),
    height=500,
    margin=dict(t=100),
)

show_plotly(fig)
```

The contrast confirms something important: The model is useful as a continuous estimator of operating regime, but it should not be read as a direct replacement for point measurements. For $J_{c}$ a fairly defensible signal appears, since the model underestimates the total fill by around 2.9 percentage points, with a mean absolute error close to 3.2 points and a moderate positive correlation. Operationally, this suggests that the reconstruction captures part of the coarse dynamics of the fill level, although its bias should be corrected if it is to be used as an absolute indicator. For $J_{b}$, by contrast, the average bias is small, but the point-to-point correlation is weak and negative; this is to be expected, because the ball level is inferred from an internal balance, pressure, and wear/replenishment assumptions, not measured directly and continuously. The ratio $J_{b}/J_{c}$ amplifies both effects, since it tends to end up overestimated and shows greater dispersion. The metallurgical reading is therefore rather prudent: We can use $J_{c}$ as a continuous tracking signal, $J_{b}$ as a trend indicator subject to recalibration, and the filling ratio as a control variable for comparing campaigns and building operating surfaces, not as an absolute number for making fine decisions without recent field contrast.

## Final comments

The exercise above does not claim to turn a SAG mill into a perfectly observable system. That would be selling smoke with pretty equations. What it does allow is something considerably more useful for operations: Building a continuous, traceable, and debatable reading of the mill's internal state from signals that normally already exist in the plant. In that sense, the value of the model lies not only in estimating $J_{c}$, $J_{b}$, or the $J_{b}/J_{c}$ ratio, but in transforming scattered variables such as power, pressure, throughput, campaign history, and point measurements into a coherent operational narrative.

The main practical gain appears when we stop looking at each signal separately. Power provides information about energy demand and charge condition; pressure helps interpret how that charge is settling; throughput shows the metallurgical consequence; and the filling ratio lets us connect all those elements with a physical hypothesis about the balance between balls, slurry, and rock. By crossing these variables on control surfaces, we no longer ask only whether the mill is drawing more or less power, but in which operating zone that power effectively translates into higher throughput.

There is also an important caveat. Models of this kind are sensitive to data quality, to the consistency of the campaigns, to major shutdowns, to ore changes, to classification conditions, and to any operational event that alters the normal relationship between power, pressure, and internal charge. For that reason, rather than thinking of this model as a closed instrument, it is best to treat it as a living analytical layer: It is calibrated with field measurements, reviewed with metallurgical judgment, updated when operating conditions change, and used to guide technical conversations, not to replace them.

From an applied standpoint, the natural next step would be to turn this logic into a per-campaign monitoring dashboard. There we could track the evolution of $J_{c}$, $J_{b}$, $J_{b}/J_{c}$, power, pressure, and throughput in a single view; detect deviations from the historical envelope; and suggest recommended operating zones under certain stability, availability, and treatment constraints. The beauty of it is that the model does not deliver a single recipe, but a map: A way of locating where the mill is operating, how far it is from its historically favorable zones, and which hypotheses are worth discussing before touching the operation.

In short, this article shows a way of moving from noisy industrial data toward an operational diagnostic tool. It is not magic, nor does it claim to be. It is simplified physical modeling, applied statistics, and process judgment put into conversation with one another. And when those three things are arranged well, even an imperfect estimate can become a very good compass for operating better.
